summary.one_line: A genuinely profitable, debt-free, certification-heavy maker of fire-suppression equipment (No.2 in India, largest exporter per CRISIL) -- but this Rs 712 crore issue is 100% promoter OFS, follows ~Rs 280 crore of buybacks and dividends to the family, and arrives as FY26 profit growth slowed to 6% with margins, working capital and capacity utilisation all moving the wrong way.
bull_points: Real quality markers: FY26 revenue from operations Rs 4,892.81 mn, operating EBITDA margin 30.75%, RoE 30.17%, RoCE 40.33%, and zero fund-based borrowings in every period presented (S1).

Certification-led position: CRISIL ranks it India's second-largest fire protection equipment maker by revenue and largest exporter (FY25); it holds 22 UL Listed and 87 FM Approved certifications, the most among focused Indian peers, and was the first Indian maker with UL-listed deluge valves (1996) (S1, S2).

Diversified revenue: 2,066 customers in FY26 with no top-5 concentration disclosed as material ('Not applicable'), ~35% exports across 90+ countries, and over 86% of FY25 revenue from repeat customers (S1, S5).
Order book of Rs 1,586.01 mn at 30 June 2026, more than double the Rs 703.45 mn at March 2025 (S4, S2).
Cash conversion is decent: operating cash flow Rs 924.92 mn in FY26 and Rs 983.15 mn in FY25 against PAT of Rs 1,167.87 mn and Rs 1,097.18 mn (S1).
bear_points: 100% offer for sale: the company receives nothing; the two oldest promoters sell 2.63 crore shares, Kusum Dharamshi selling about 55% of her holding, at a weighted average acquisition cost of Rs 0.05-0.09 per share (S1, S4).

Cash already extracted pre-IPO: buybacks of ~Rs 83 crore from related parties in FY23-FY24, then dividends of Rs 56.15 crore in FY25 and Rs 140.18 crore in FY26; the FY26 dividend exceeded FY26 profit, so net worth fell (S2, S10, S1).
Growth is slowing: FY26 PAT grew only 6.4% on 13% revenue growth, and Q1 FY27 EBITDA margin fell to 27.26% from 30.75% (S1, S7).
About a third of revenue is contract-manufactured goods, mostly imported, and China supplied 29.19% of FY25 purchases, which weakens the 'Indian manufacturer' framing (S2, S11).
Governance flag: a joint statutory auditor resigned before the end of their term and was then appointed CFO, which the RHP lists as a top-10 risk (S1).
watch_points: Whether the Rs 1,586 mn June-2026 order book converts into FY27 revenue at FY25-level margins (S4, S1).
Working capital: the cash conversion cycle went from 83 days (FY25) to 102 days (FY26) and 112 days (Q1 FY27, computed on a quarterly basis) (S1).
Capacity utilisation: Jalgaon foam utilisation fell to 63.40% in FY26 and gas suppression produced nothing, with gas revenue going to zero (S11, S1).
Execution of the Saudi Arabia local manufacturing and trading plan with a shortlisted partner within 1-2 years (S2, S12).
Day-2 and day-3 subscription split, especially genuine QIB demand beyond the Rs 213 crore anchor book (S8).

reasoning: The money does nothing for the business: the issue is 100% OFS, so not a rupee funds capacity, the Saudi plan or R&D. Post-issue, the company is the same debt-free, self-funding entity, and the only change is that promoters convert about 15% of equity into cash (S1, S4).

The moat is real but narrow. A certification and empanelment barrier (22 UL / 87 FM approvals, Aramco 9COM vendor numbers, 6-24 months to certify new products) protects it from unorganised players. It is not a technology monopoly: Safex, Newage, Vimal, Johnson Controls and others hold UL/FM approvals in overlapping categories, and roughly 36% of revenue is bought-in contract-manufactured product (S2, S1).

Business quality is high but the trend has turned. Revenue CAGR was 14.5% over FY24-FY26, but PAT growth slowed to 6.4% in FY26, EBITDA margin slipped to 27.26% in Q1 FY27, inventory and receivable days lengthened, and two product lines (gas suppression, custom systems) shrank sharply. Applying today means paying for growth that the latest numbers do not yet confirm (S1, S4).

Promoter conduct is the main governance concern, not illegality. RPTs are mostly remuneration, buybacks and dividends with no promoter-linked supplier or customer entities. But the family took ~Rs 280 crore out via buybacks and dividends before selling Rs 712 crore in the OFS, promoter-director pay rose to ~Rs 29 crore (6.7% of FY25 revenue), and an ex-auditor became CFO (S2, S10, S1).

Litigation and compliance risk is minimal: nothing is outstanding against the company or promoters, and there are only three small tax matters filed by the company, worth Rs 0.40 mn. So this is not an 'avoid' on red flags (S1).

Net: a good business sold at the wrong moment of its own cycle by sellers who have already been paid. Track it for two to three quarters of listed disclosures (order-book conversion, margin recovery, working capital, Saudi progress) rather than applying in the IPO (S1, S4, S12).

subsections.title: What HD Fire makes and how it earns revenue

blocks.text: HD Fire Protect is a Mumbai/Thane-based maker of fire suppression equipment (water, foam and gas based), the hardware that sits inside a sprinkler or deluge system rather than detection or alarm electronics. The business started as H.D. Fire Protect Company, a partnership set up by Harish Dharamshi in April 1990. The company was incorporated in April 1997 and took over the partnership as a going concern on 1 April 2005 (S2). It sells across eight product categories: sprinklers, alarm valves and accessories; deluge valves, deluge skids and pre-action systems; foam equipment and suppression systems; monitors and monitor nozzles; system valves and accessories; water spray nozzles; custom engineered systems; and gas suppression systems (S1).

blocks.caption: Revenue from operations by product (Rs million; excludes export incentives and scrap) (S1)

blocks.text: Revenue is earned by product sale, not by contracting or annuity service. Three categories (sprinklers/alarm valves, deluge systems and foam) were about 75% of FY26 revenue, and these drove the growth. Deluge revenue grew roughly 24% and foam roughly 22% in FY26, per our computation from (S1). Two lines went the other way: gas suppression fell from Rs 87.51 mn in FY24 to nil in FY26, and custom engineered systems fell from Rs 85.74 mn to Rs 35.20 mn in FY26 (S1). The 'comprehensive portfolio' pitch is therefore partly historical, because one of the eight categories currently earns nothing.

Customers are industrial and infrastructure buyers in oil and gas, refining and petrochemicals, power, heavy engineering, aerospace, pharmaceuticals, data centres and warehousing, plus commercial and residential buildings (S1). Reference projects named in the offer documents include master stream nozzles at the Sriharikota launch pad, equipment at the Jamnagar refinery and the new Parliament building, deluge valves for Saudi Aramco's Ras Tanura Sea Island, and Oman's Integrated Power & Water Plant (S2, S6).

Customer concentration is low. The abridged prospectus marks revenue concentration among the top five customers as 'Not applicable' (S1), the customer count was 2,066 in FY26 (S1), and over 86% of FY25 revenue came from repeat customers (S5). That is a genuine positive: no single EPC contractor or end-user can squeeze margins or take the business away. The flip side is a falling customer count, from 2,179 in FY25 to 2,066 in FY26 (S1), alongside 13% revenue growth, so growth is coming from larger tickets rather than a widening base.

Go-to-market is distributor-led abroad and stockist-led in India (S2). In the last three years the company appointed new distributors in Colombia, Argentina, South Africa, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Malaysia (S2). Its Jalgaon unit holds Saudi Aramco 9COM vendor numbers for valves and sprinkler systems, which lets it receive RFQs for Aramco projects in those categories (S2). Credit terms run up to 150 days for some customers, and some sales go through middlemen, which the DRHP flags as a collection risk (S2).

Exports are a large and steady 33-36% of revenue, but FY26 export growth (about 8.5%, computed from S1) lagged domestic growth (about 16%), and Rest of Asia revenue fell. The 'largest exporter' claim is about scale, not momentum.

subsections.title: Manufacturing footprint, capacity and supply chain

blocks.text: The company runs two plants in Maharashtra, at Jalgaon MIDC and Thane MIDC, on a combined 8.50 acres (S1). Jalgaon is the vertically integrated site, with an in-house non-ferrous foundry, an ASME-certified fabrication shop for U-stamp pressure vessels, CNC/VMC machining including 5-axis centres, and flow testing up to 18,000 litres per minute. Thane makes water spray nozzles (S2). A Jalgaon extension of 2.50 acres (manufacturing plus fire test lab, warehouse and R&D centre) has been added, and a 0.50-acre warehouse at Wagle Estate, Thane is due by November 2026 (S1). The DRHP said these projects would be funded from internal accruals, with Rs 38.91 mn spent by March 2025 and a further Rs 230 mn planned (S2).

blocks.caption: Installed capacity and utilisation, Jalgaon and Thane (EPU = equivalent production unit) (S2; FY26 from S11)

blocks.text: Supply chain: the key inputs are ductile iron, cast iron and cast steel castings, forgings, steel pipes and fittings, copper and stainless tubing, brass and bronze valves, gauges, elastomers and paints (S2). Much of the finished product is bought in, not made. Contract-manufactured products were 33.02% of FY25 revenue (S2) and about 36.5% in FY26, since own plants accounted for 63.49% (S1). Imported contract-manufactured goods alone were 28.46% of total expenses in FY25. Partners are in China, Hong Kong, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan and India, and China supplied 29.19% of FY25 purchases (S2). The top-10 suppliers rose from 35.59% of total expenses in FY24 to 42.90% in FY25, 47.76% in FY26 and 59.28% in Q1 FY27, all without long-term contracts (S1). Named large suppliers include Daejin Sanup Vietnam, Pearl Cast Alloys, KV Fire Chemicals India, Protector Safety Ind. Co, Mala Metals and Potter Hong Kong; the single largest supplier (10.11% of FY25 expenses) was not named for lack of consent (S2).

FY26 foam revenue rose about 22% while Jalgaon foam production fell from 41,129 to 30,659 EPUs (S1, S11). Our inference is that more foam product was bought in or the mix shifted. Either way, rising supplier concentration plus falling own-plant utilisation suggests the company is leaning more on trading and contract manufacturing.

Per the CRISIL report commissioned and paid for by the company, India's fire protection equipment market grew at a 12% CAGR from FY20 to FY26, reaching Rs 109 billion. It is expected to grow at 10-12% a year to Rs 175-195 billion by FY31. Fire suppression (sprinklers, hydrants, deluge valves, gas systems, foam) was 75% of the market at Rs 82 billion in FY26 and is projected at 11-13% CAGR to Rs 135-155 billion (S1). India's per capita spend on fire protection equipment is about US$1, against US$57 in North America and US$52 in Europe (S1).

Demand drivers cited are stricter fire codes, data centres, warehousing, refineries and petrochemicals, and Gulf infrastructure. CRISIL also lists import substitution as an opportunity, and economic slowdown, regulatory change and raw-material volatility as threats (S2, S5). On FY26 revenue of Rs 4,892.81 mn, HD Fire's implied share of the Rs 109 bn total market is roughly 4.5% (our computation from S1). It is a leader in a fragmented market, not a dominant player.
The industry data comes from a single company-paid report (CRISIL), which is standard for Indian IPOs. Treat growth projections as directional, not as independent forecasts.

CRISIL describes the industry as a few large multinationals (Honeywell, Johnson Controls) plus branded domestic players, together about 70% of the market, with local and unbranded players making up the remaining 30%. Siemens, Viking and Victaulic are also present (S2). Named focused domestic peers are Safex Fire Services, Newage Fire Fighting Company, Ceasefire Industries, De's Technico, Vimal Fire Controls, Firetech Equipment & Systems and Fluid Pumps & Equipment. Diversified players are Johnson Controls (India), Honeywell (India) and Gunnebo India (S2). None of the listed 'peers' the RHP uses for comparison (Azad Engineering, KSB, Ingersoll-Rand, Elgi, Kirloskar Pneumatic) is a pure fire-protection company (S5).

blocks.caption: Export revenue of select competitors, FY24 (Rs million) (S2)

blocks.text: Competition is product-by-product rather than head-on. Per CRISIL's offering map, HD Fire is the only domestic player present in all eight suppression categories. Safex covers five, overlapping in sprinklers, foam, valves, deluge and gas; Newage overlaps in sprinklers, foam, valves, spray nozzles and monitors (S2). In sprinklers and deluge valves, it also competes with global brands that hold the same UL/FM approvals.

There is a genuine but moderate barrier: certification and vendor empanelment. UL and FM approval for a new product typically takes 6-24 months and is maintained through quarterly audits by UL Solutions and FM Approvals. Empanelment with large customers takes 3-12 months and includes on-site audits (S2). HD Fire holds 22 UL Listed and 87 FM Approved certifications, the highest count among focused Indian peers. It is also the only focused peer holding UL, FM, CE, VdS, ASME-U and Lloyd's Register across its categories (S2). There are specific 'firsts': the first Indian maker with UL-listed deluge valves (1996), the first with FM approval for low-expansion foam system components, the first to get an ASME U-stamp in this space, and, as of September 2025, the only Indian maker of a UL-listed pre-action system (S2). It also holds patents in India, the US and Saudi Arabia for a pressure-operated fluid valve (S2).

What the moat is not: it is not a regulatory monopoly or a sole-source import-substitution position. Safex, Newage, Vimal, Fluid Pumps and Johnson Controls all hold UL and/or FM approvals in overlapping categories (S2). The company also buys roughly a third of what it sells from contract manufacturers, largely in China and East Asia (S2, S1). Anyone with a UL-listed product and a distributor could bid against that portion. The certification stack raises the cost of entry for unorganised players and supports the high margins, but it does not stop well-capitalised multinationals or certified domestic rivals.

Moat verdict: a real but narrow certification and empanelment barrier, plus a track record on reference projects (Aramco, Jamnagar). It is better than most small-cap industrial IPOs, but it is not a structural monopoly.

blocks.caption: Restated financial summary (Rs million) (S1; FY23 from S2)

blocks.text: The three-year record is strong. Revenue grew at a 14.54% CAGR from FY24 to FY26 (S4), and PAT rose from Rs 879.20 mn to Rs 1,167.87 mn (S1), about a 15% CAGR by our computation. The shape matters more than the average, though. FY25 was the peak year: revenue grew about 16% and PAT about 25%, with EBITDA margin expanding to 31.89%. FY26 revenue grew 13%, but PAT grew only 6.4% and EBITDA margin fell to 30.75% (S1, S7). Q1 FY27 margin fell further, to 27.26% EBITDA and 20.92% PAT (S1). There is no Q1 FY26 comparative in the documents we read, so seasonality cannot be ruled out. Still, the direction of travel at the point of IPO is decelerating profit and compressing margin.

The growth story sold in the prospectus leans on the FY23-FY25 trajectory. The two most recent periods (FY26 and Q1 FY27) show slowing profit growth and lower margins, so the trend does not cleanly support the narrative.

The balance sheet is clean in the usual sense: zero fund-based borrowings in every period (S1). The only contingent liability disclosed at March 2025 was Rs 57.94 mn of bank guarantees, fully secured against fixed deposits (S2). Equity share capital rose from Rs 26.55 mn to Rs 876.15 mn in FY25 purely through bonus issues (2:1 in November 2023 and July 2024, 10:1 in March 2025) and a split from Rs 100 to Rs 5 face value. No new money came in (S2).

Working capital is the weak spot. The cash conversion cycle improved to 83 days in FY25, then lengthened to 102 days in FY26 as both inventory days (77 to 85) and receivable days (45 to 57) rose (S1). The Q1 FY27 figures (109 inventory days, 112-day cycle) are computed on a quarter basis and are not strictly comparable, but they point the same way (S1). Net worth fell in FY26, from Rs 3,972.32 mn to Rs 3,771.47 mn, despite Rs 1,167.87 mn of profit, because the company paid Rs 140.18 crore in dividends, more than the year's PAT (S1, S10).

blocks.caption: Operating cash flow vs profit (Rs million) (S1)

blocks.text: There is no alarming cash/profit mismatch. Operating cash flow covered 73-90% of PAT across FY24-FY26, and was strong in Q1 FY27 (S1). The FY26 dip relative to FY25, with CFO down while PAT rose, is consistent with the lengthening working capital cycle. FY26 cash generated from operations before tax was Rs 133.08 crore, and taxes paid were Rs 40.59 crore (S10). Cash and cash equivalents were only Rs 14.87 crore at March 2026, plus Rs 4.57 crore of other bank balances (S10). Most surplus cash went to shareholders rather than staying on the balance sheet.

Data inconsistency: the abridged prospectus summary table shows FY26 investing cash flow at Rs (1,360.58) mn and financing at Rs 409.74 mn (S1). A line-by-line read of the RHP cash flow statement reports the reverse: a financing outflow of Rs 136.06 crore, consistent with the Rs 140.18 crore dividend, and an investing inflow of Rs 40.97 crore (S10). We treat the summary table as transposed for FY26, but could not open the full RHP to confirm.

blocks.text: The DRHP was dated 24 September 2025 (S2) and reported filed with SEBI in September 2025 (S17); the issue opening on 13 October was also reported by (S18). SEBI's observations were reported issued on 29 January 2026 (S19), and the RHP is dated 5 October 2026 (S1, S3). Some secondary sources (S9, S14) state the NII share as 10% rather than 15%. The 15% figure in (S4, S7) is the standard split of the net offer, and the difference is likely an employee-reservation carve-out. Readers should rely on the RHP's 'Offer Structure' section.

subsections.title: Objects of the issue: where the money goes

blocks.text: The stated objects are (i) to carry out the offer for sale and (ii) to achieve the benefits of listing. The company will not receive any proceeds; all proceeds, net of offer expenses and taxes, go to the two promoter selling shareholders in proportion to the shares they sell (S1). There is no capex, debt repayment, working capital or general corporate purpose component, because there is no fresh issue. Offer-related costs borne for the selling shareholders were Rs 6.98 crore by 30 June 2026 (S10).

An OFS raises nothing for the company. Expansion (Jalgaon, Thane, Saudi Arabia) will continue to be funded from internal accruals, as it would have been without the IPO. Investors are buying shares from 70- and 72-year-old promoters with an average cost of under Rs 0.10 per share. Kusum Dharamshi is selling more than half her stake.

Promoter and promoter-group holding goes from 100% to about 85% post-issue (S4), so the family keeps firm control and the free float is only 15%. Within three years before the RHP, there were no share transactions at a price; all movements were bonuses, gifts or splits (S1, S2).

Harish Narshi Dharamshi (72), Chairman and MD, is a mechanical engineer (B.V.B. College, Karnatak University). He founded the predecessor partnership in 1990 and has over 36 years in the fire protection industry (S1). Kusum Harish Dharamshi (70) is a promoter but not an operating executive. She was an academic (vice principal and director of academics at Kum. U.R. Shah Women's College of Commerce from 1977 to 2014) (S1). The next generation are whole-time directors. Miheer Ghotikar (44) is a biomedical engineer, formerly with Pilgrim Software and Baxter in the US. Parika Ghotikar (43) is a mechanical engineer, formerly with Deloitte & Touche Consulting (USA). Anik Dharamshi (42) is a mechanical engineer with over 16 years at the company (S1).

The board has eight directors, four of them independent (including one woman): Navin Muthu Ram, Sudha Ravi, Nagesh Dinkar Pinge and Ramesh Chandak. The CFO is Hitesh Dedhia, and the Company Secretary is Sundaram Balasubramanian Iyer (S1). The track record is long and the promoters are fire-protection specialists with no other listed ventures disclosed. However, management is entirely family, and the operating second generation has about 16 years of industry experience each (S1, S2).

The RHP lists among its top-10 risks that one of the joint statutory auditors resigned before completing their term and was later appointed CFO (S1). This is not illegal, but it blurs the line between the auditor and the audited. It deserves more weight than a boilerplate risk.

blocks.caption: Key related-party flows (Rs million) (S2 for FY23-FY25; S10 for FY26)
rows: Buyback of shares from promoters/relatives (computed total)

blocks.text: The RPT section is clean of the typical red flags. We found no promoter-owned supplier or customer entities, no related-party loans, and no common-directorship trading counterparties (S2). Related-party flows are almost entirely three kinds of payments to family members: salaries, share buybacks (FY23-FY24) and dividends (FY25-FY26). The FY26 related-party dividends of Rs 140.19 crore went mostly to Harish (Rs 78.68 crore), Kusum (Rs 24.99 crore), Miheer (Rs 14.71 crore), Parika (Rs 9.28 crore) and Anik (Rs 5.97 crore) (S10). Professional fees paid to Hiren Dharamshi, a relative, were trivial at Rs 0.60 mn in FY25 (S2).

The amounts are large, though. By our computation from (S2), whole-time director pay jumped from about Rs 168 mn in FY24 to about Rs 291 mn in FY25, around 6.7% of revenue and over a quarter of PAT, in the year before the DRHP was filed. Across FY23-FY26, the family took roughly Rs 280 crore out through buybacks and dividends (S2, S10), before selling Rs 712 crore of stock in this OFS. None of this is irregular; it is the family's money. But it shows that the pre-IPO period was used to monetise the business, not to reinvest in it.

Litigation is genuinely immaterial. Nothing is pending against the company or its promoters, there is no SEBI or stock-exchange disciplinary action against the promoters, and the company's own three tax matters total Rs 0.40 mn (S1). Two criminal proceedings name non-promoter directors; the abridged prospectus does not quantify them. The statutory auditors' report on the restated financials carries no qualifications or adverse remarks (S1). We found no reports of delayed filings or regulatory notices in the documents and coverage we reviewed.

items: Supplier concentration and import dependence. Top-10 suppliers rose from 35.59% of total expenses in FY24 to 59.28% in Q1 FY27, with no long-term contracts. China was 29.19% of FY25 purchases, and imported contract-manufactured goods were 28.46% of FY25 expenses. A trade restriction or tariff on Chinese fire equipment would hit both cost and availability (S1, S2).

Product liability. A failed sprinkler or deluge valve can mean loss of life. The standard 24-month warranty excludes consequential damages, but tort and strict-liability claims can still arise. The company reports no recalls and a 0.01% replacement rate so far (S2).

Certification dependence. Losing or failing to renew UL/FM approvals, which are audited quarterly, would shut it out of export and insurer-specified projects. Certification costs rose from Rs 11.07 mn in FY23 to Rs 24.52 mn in FY25 (S2).

Export and Gulf exposure. About a third of revenue is exported, with the Middle East the largest overseas region at 14.98% of FY26 revenue. This brings exposure to geopolitics, currency, and local-standards protectionism (S1, S2).

blocks.text: Of these, supplier concentration is the one moving in the wrong direction fastest, and it compounds the 'how much is really made in-house' question raised in the business section (S1, S2).

items: Under-utilisation and product-line erosion. Foam utilisation fell to 63.40% and gas suppression output to zero in FY26, while new Jalgaon and Thane capacity is being added. Fixed costs rise before demand is proven (S11, S1).
Working capital stretch. The cash conversion cycle lengthened to 102 days in FY26, and credit terms run up to 150 days, with some sales routed through middlemen (S1, S2).
Single-state plant concentration. Both plants are in Maharashtra, generating 63.49% of FY26 revenue, and Jalgaon is far from ports, which raises export logistics cost (S1, S2).

Governance. The ex-auditor-turned-CFO, the high promoter remuneration and the cash extraction pre-IPO mean minority shareholders need to watch capital allocation once the family holds 85% (S1, S2, S10).
No new capital and a small float. The company gets nothing from the IPO, and the 15% free float leaves the stock exposed to supply overhang if promoters sell more after lock-in (S1, S4).

blocks.text: Generic risks repeated in every prospectus (Indian GAAP differences, macro slowdown, labour laws) are omitted here as non-decisive.

The concrete forward statements come from the offer documents, not from investor calls or interviews; we found no management interview (S12). They cover four strategies: (1) product innovation, including fluorine-free foam systems and a pressure-reducing deluge valve pursuing UL listing; (2) capacity expansion at Jalgaon and Thane, funded internally (Rs 230 mn planned over 12 months per the DRHP); (3) more international certifications, particularly FM approvals; and (4) geographic expansion (S1, S2).

The most specific plan is Saudi Arabia: a local manufacturing and trading presence within one to two years with a shortlisted partner, subject to approvals. The aim is to meet localisation requirements and qualify for large government projects (S2, S12). The company also targets Southeast Asia, Middle East and South Asian government infrastructure, data centres and warehouses (S2). No revenue or margin guidance is given anywhere in the material we read.
No quantified guidance exists. Any FY27 growth estimate would be an extrapolation, not a management statement.

subsections.title: What the hard data says about the near term

blocks.text: The strongest forward indicator is the order book: Rs 1,586.01 mn at 30 June 2026 (S4, S5), against Rs 703.45 mn at March 2025, Rs 752.92 mn at March 2024 and Rs 608.73 mn at March 2023 (S2). That is about a third of annual revenue, and its doubling is the best evidence for FY27 growth. The offsetting evidence is Q1 FY27 revenue of Rs 1,090.52 mn, below the FY26 quarterly average of about Rs 1,223 mn (our computation), at a lower 27.26% EBITDA margin (S1). The order-book jump may also reflect larger, project-type orders with longer execution and lower margins, though the documents do not say so explicitly.

items: Positive: a larger order book, data-centre and warehousing demand, and Gulf infrastructure spend (S4, S2).
Negative: softer margins, lengthening working capital, and declining gas and custom-systems lines (S1).
Unknown: the timing and economics of the Saudi venture, and whether new capacity lifts own-manufacturing share or adds idle fixed cost (S2, S12).

subsections.title: Anchor book, day-1 status and grey market

blocks.text: The anchor book raised Rs 213.11 crore on 12 October 2026, allotting 78.64 lakh shares to 25 funds at Rs 271, the top of the band (S8). Named anchors include Bajaj Life Insurance, Axis Max Life Insurance, Allianz Global Investors Fund, Kotak MF, ICICI Prudential MF, Aditya Birla Sun Life MF, HDFC MF, Mirae Asset MF, UTI MF and Bandhan MF (S8). Lock-in dates were not given in the sources we opened; SEBI's standard staggered anchor lock-in applies.

This report is written on day 1 (13 October 2026). As of writing, no credible category-wise subscription data (QIB/NII/retail) was available. Trackers either showed pre-opening placeholders of 0.00x or had not updated since 12 October (S15, S14, S16). We therefore report no subscription multiple. Subscription closes 15 October (S1).

Grey market premium (unofficial, unregulated): IPO Ji reported Rs 82 at 6:45 am on 13 Oct 2026 (S13), and InvestorGain Rs 86 on 13 Oct (S14). Both were around Rs 60-70 a week earlier. GMP is not an investment signal and played no part in our verdict.

method: Primary sources: (1) the SEBI-hosted Abridged Prospectus summarising the RHP dated 5 Oct 2026. It was read in full (11 pages): restated financials to June 2026, KPIs, revenue by product and geography, promoters, shareholding, top-10 risk factors and the litigation table.
